analysis.one_liner: Lets workers unionize by signed cards instead of elections, and forces arbitration for stalled first contracts.
analysis.headline: Introduced in October 2015 with 11 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how workers form unions. Today, workers must win a secret-ballot election overseen by the National Labor Relations Board, and after winning they often wait years for a first contract because an employer can bargain in bad faith with no penalty. The bill would let the Board certify a union directly once a majority of workers signs cards saying they want one, skipping the election. If bargaining for a first contract stalls, it would move to mediation after 90 days and then to binding arbitration, meaning a third party would set the contract terms for two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to join a union. Skipping the election avoids the long, employer-driven campaigns that often follow a filing, and mandatory arbitration guarantees that a newly formed union gets an enforceable first contract instead of bargaining that can drag on for years.

how_it_helps.text: The National Labor Relations Board would have to certify a union without an election if a majority of workers in a bargaining unit signed valid authorization cards and no other union is already recognized, eliminating the election stage where employers often campaign against the union. [S2] [S3]

For a first contract, the parties would have to meet within 10 days of a request; either side could call in a federal mediator after 90 days; and if mediation did not produce agreement within 30 more days, the dispute would go to an arbitration board whose decision binds both parties for two years. [S2] [S3]

Binding first-contract arbitration closes the gap workers face today, where the law requires the employer to bargain but imposes no penalty for never agreeing, so a union can exist on paper for years without a contract. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially those resisting unionization. They lose the chance to run an anti-union campaign before an election, and if they cannot reach a first contract, an arbitrator would set wages and working conditions for them. Most workers who do not seek to unionize would see little direct change.

drawbacks.text: Card-check certification replaces the secret ballot with signed authorization cards collected in the workplace, so workers would cast their choice in front of coworkers and union organizers rather than in private; defenders of elections argue this raises the risk of pressure on signers. [S3]

Mandatory first-contract arbitration means a government-appointed arbitration board, not the employer or the workers' own bargaining leverage, would set the actual terms of wages and working conditions for at least two years, taking a core decision out of both sides' hands. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers seeking union representation, the bill fixes two real bottlenecks: the employer campaign before an election and the years-long stall before a first contract. The trade-off is real but narrow: it removes the privacy of the ballot in the organizing stage and substitutes an arbitrator's judgment for negotiated agreement when talks fail. Neither drawback touches workers who never organize, and both apply only at the moment a union is being formed or a first contract is being set.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee on the same day, and the committee never acted on it; it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2017 with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on October 6, 2015, joined by ten Democratic cosponsors listed at introduction, including Sherrod Brown, Patty Murray, Elizabeth Warren, Kirsten Gillibrand, and Ron Wyden-era colleagues such as Tom Heinrich, Debbie Stabenow, Mazie Hirono, Patrick Leahy, and Sheldon Whitehouse. [S3] [S4]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. [S1] [S5]
That referral was the bill's last action of record; the action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor scheduling, and no roll call for the remainder of the 114th Congress. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced card-check certification and mandatory first-contract arbitration keep the current system, in which they can run election campaigns against unions and legally stall first contracts for years. The twelve senators who sponsored and cosponsored it gain a platform piece but no policy change, and workers gain nothing.

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Workplace Democracy Act and assigned it to the Senate labor committee.

for.name: 11 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a full slate of party support but no Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the referral stage.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; with no committee action, it never reached a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All twelve sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Sanders, who caucuses with Democrats; there were no Republican cosponsors, and the bill never advanced past the Republican-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Employers, especially nonunion companies facing organizing drives
industries.note: Card-check certification removes the election campaign employers use to argue against unions, and mandatory first-contract arbitration means an arbitrator can set their wages and work rules if bargaining stalls. The cost falls on companies that would have preferred to remain nonunion.

Certification by signed cards makes organizing far faster and cheaper, and guaranteed first contracts turn new units into functioning bargaining relationships. Union growth depends on exactly these two steps.
